source.filename: 2021-flexible seft-power multifunctional sensor for stiffness-tunable soft robotic gripper by multimaterial 3D printing.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Dominance of the in-plane piezoelectric effect during initial bending (curvature below 5.3 m^-1) followed by additional out-of-plane piezoelectric compression at larger bending curvatures.
Piecewise linear approximation between output voltage and bending curvature as an accurate representation for sensing purposes despite potential nonlinearities.
Linear relationship between initial bending stiffness and sensor output voltage under constant vacuum pressure.
Nonlinear resisting force-displacement response of the soft finger across different inflation and vacuum pressure states.
Viscoelastic behavior noted for unstructured elastomeric layers contributing to slow relaxation after load removal.
control_variables: Linear motor moving speed and pulling speed controlled at 1 mm/s
Soft finger geometry with nine pneumatic inflation chambers and a 2 mm strain-limiting layer
PVDF film thickness (110 µm) and piezoelectric coefficients (d33 = 33 pC/N, d31 = 23 pC/N)
Object weight used in pick-and-place validation (200 g toy lemon)
Horizontal manipulation speed of the industrial robotic arm (0.4 m/s)
Cyclic pressure test amplitude (30 kPa) and cycle count (400 cycles)
dependent_variables: Contact-point strain from finite element simulation
Open-circuit voltage and closed-circuit current of the sensor
Bending curvature (inverse of radius of curvature)
Initial bending stiffness of the finger
Sensor sensitivities (pressure sensitivity, curvature sensitivity, stiffness sensitivity)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Integrating 3D-printed microstructured patterns onto jamming layers enhances piezoelectric pressure sensitivity, with soft trigonal line-shaped structures achieving 0.38 V/kPa under 7 kPa due to elevated strain and contact area deformation.

An embedded self-powered PVDF sensor passively detects soft finger bending curvature in two piecewise linear sensitivity regimes (0.12 mV·m below 5.3 m^-1 and 0.55 mV·m above 5.3 m^-1) governed by in-plane and out-of-plane piezoelectric mechanisms.

Vacuum-actuated layer jamming modulates finger initial stiffness between 15 N/m and 44 N/m and increases resisting force up to approximately 6.5 N, with initial stiffness correlating linearly with sensor voltage output at a sensitivity of approximately 0.09 V·m/N.

Multimaterial 3D printing enables monolithic fabrication of a soft pneumatic finger body, hard reinforcement structures, airtight double O-ring connectors, and variable-stiffness jamming layers housing a flexible piezoelectric thin film.

A three-finger soft robotic gripper equipped with embedded jamming-sensing layers can record distinct voltage peaks during dynamic wrapping (~1 V) and vacuum stiffening (~2 V) throughout a 10-step pick-and-place routine without external sensor power.

experimental_setup: Commercial multimaterial 3D printer (Objet350, Stratasys) utilizing TangoPlus (finger body), Vero PureWhite (reinforcement), FLX9760 (double O-rings), RGD8530 (jamming layers), and FLX9840 (soft microstructures)
Piezoelectric sensor fabricated from polarized 110 µm PVDF thin film with silver electrodes bonded using silver paste
Olympus IX83 microscope for optical characterization of printed microstructures
Keithley 6514 high-input-impedance electrometer (> 200 TΩ input impedance, < 1 fA noise) for measuring open-circuit voltage and closed-circuit current
Motorized linear stage (SURUGA SEIKI KZG06030-CA) with an IMADA ZTS-50N strain gauge driven at 1 mm/s for cyclic compression tests
Pneumatic control system comprising an air pump with positive pressure regulator (ITV2050-212BS) and a vacuum pump with negative pressure regulator (ITV2090-212BS5)
Camera positioned above the finger for optical bending curvature tracking
Motorized positioner (SURUGA SEIKI KXL06200) with a force gauge for mid-position resisting force characterization (displacements up to 10 mm at 1 mm/s)
Three-finger gripper mounted to an industrial robotic arm performing a 10-step pick-and-place operation on a 200 g toy lemon at 0.4 m/s
future_work: Developing sensors with ultra-low power consumption to expand applications and tackle energy efficiency limitations in flexible sensors
Implementing self-powered sensing approaches to eliminate dependence on externally powered sensors for condition monitoring in robotics
Advancing anthropomorphic grippers capable of safe, friendly interaction through integrated variable stiffness and perception
independent_variables: Surface geometry of the sensitive-enhancing jamming layer (flat, square line-shaped, trigonal line-shaped)
Material stiffness of the surface patterns (hard RGD8530 vs soft FLX9840)
Load resistance for power output characterization (10^7 Ω to 5 × 10^9 Ω)
limitations_inferred: Because the sensing mechanism is piezoelectric and signals dissipate over time, the sensor cannot continuously measure static bending curvature or static stiffness under prolonged hold conditions without dynamic excitation.

During combined actuation states, the voltage signal reflects coupled contributions of curvature prestrain and stiffness, requiring sequential or decoupled procedures rather than independent simultaneous readout.
Cyclic durability of the 3D-printed jamming interface and PVDF bonding was evaluated only up to 400 compression cycles, leaving long-term fatigue under repeated large-strain bending uncharacterized.
Manipulation experiments were demonstrated on a single object of fixed mass and geometry without demonstrating closed-loop feedback control based on the sensor signals.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Multimaterial 3D printing suffers from geometric inaccuracies and poor surface finish due to slicing of tessellated models and layer-by-layer deposition, particularly on complex curved shapes.
Printed microscale patterns were unable to maintain their exact CAD-designed geometries, especially the square line-shaped patterns.
The piecewise linear curve might not fully represent the complete constitutive relationship between bending curvature and sensor voltage output.
In real grasping tasks, target object dimensions constrain finger bending before the inflation pressure reaches the commanded setpoint, producing lower voltage output than unconstrained calibration.
Voltage amplitudes varied between benchtop characterization and in-finger measurements due to differences in internal and external testing conditions.
main_results: Multimaterial 3D printing successfully integrated a nine-chamber reinforced soft finger body, sealing mechanisms, and variable-stiffness jamming layers containing a flexible piezoelectric PVDF sensor into a unified structure.

Soft trigonal line-shaped patterns achieved the highest strain under FEM simulation (3.5 times higher than flat surfaces) and delivered the highest pressure sensitivity (0.38 V/kPa below ~7 kPa and 0.06 V/kPa at higher pressures).

The piezoelectric sensor attained a maximum power output of approximately 6 nW at an optimal load resistance of 1.25 × 10^8 Ω, with stable cyclic repeatability exhibiting less than 8% voltage loss over 400 cycles at 30 kPa.

Curvature sensing demonstrated two distinct linear regimes: 0.12 mV·m below 5.3 m^-1 (dominated by in-plane piezoelectric deformation) and 0.55 mV·m above 5.3 m^-1 (boosted by out-of-plane compression).

Vacuum-driven layer jamming tuned finger initial stiffness from 15–16 N/m up to 44 N/m and resisting force up to ~6.5 N, with initial stiffness displaying a linear relationship with sensor voltage at ~0.09 V·m/N (R^2 = 0.98).

A three-finger soft gripper demonstrated successful pick-and-place manipulation of a 200 g toy lemon at 0.4 m/s, capturing dynamic finger bending (~1 V) and vacuum stiffening (~2 V) voltage peaks without requiring external power.
modeling_methods: 2D COMSOL finite element modeling (FEM) to analyze strain distributions of flat, square, and trigonal line-shaped configurations under 30 kPa pressure
Piecewise linear fitting to determine curvature sensitivities across low and high bending regimes
Linear regression analysis (R^2 = 0.98) correlating sensor voltage output with initial bending stiffness
performance_metrics: Pressure sensitivity: 0.38 V/kPa (pressure < ~7 kPa) and 0.06 V/kPa (pressure > ~7 kPa) for soft trigonal microstructures
Maximum electrical power: ~6 nW at 1.25 × 10^8 Ω load resistance
Voltage retention under cyclic pressure: 4.7% drop in area 2 and 8% drop in area 3 after 400 cycles at 30 kPa
Curvature sensitivity: 0.12 mV·m (curvature < 5.3 m^-1) and 0.55 mV·m (curvature > 5.3 m^-1)
Initial bending stiffness range: 15–44 N/m (16 N/m at zero pressure to 44 N/m at Pi = 40 kPa, Pv = -30 kPa)
Resisting force: ~2.8 N (Pi = 0 kPa, Pv = 0 kPa at 10 mm displacement), ~4.5 N (Pi = 0 kPa, Pv = -30 kPa), and ~6.5 N (Pi = 40 kPa, Pv = -30 kPa)
Grasping signal peaks: ~1 V during pneumatic bending and ~2 V during vacuum stiffening
possible_gap_implications: Because the piezoelectric effect only generates transient charges during strain rate changes and dissipates charges over time, static grasping perception and long-duration hold monitoring would require hybrid sensing or charge-drift compensation strategies.

The necessity of a two-stage sequential operation (allowing curvature signals to dissipate before applying vacuum for stiffness detection) indicates a potential gap in continuous, real-time decoupled sensing during unstructured contact interactions.
Geometric fidelity limitations in multimaterial 3D printing of microscale features suggest that manufacturing inconsistencies could cause sensor-to-sensor calibration variances in batch production.
paper.research_objective: To design, fabricate, and characterize an embedded, flexible, self-powered multifunctional sensor combining a piezoelectric PVDF film with 3D-printed microstructured jamming layers within a multimaterial 3D-printed soft robotic finger, capable of passively sensing bending curvature and initial stiffness while actively tuning finger stiffness via vacuum layer jamming without external power or impeding robotic dynamics.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic grippers require proprioceptive sensation and controllable stiffness to perform safe and dexterous grasping, but conventional rigid sensors disrupt soft robot dynamics, existing multifunctional sensors demand complex wiring layouts that increase device bulk, pneumatic fingers frequently suffer from excessive radial expansion and stress concentration, and conventional flexible sensors typically measure only a single parameter while relying on external power supplies.
paper.title: Flexible self-powered multifunctional sensor for stiffness-tunable soft robotic gripper by multimaterial 3D printing
